messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla, a 69-year-old woman of Middle Eastern descent, had worked the late shift at a fast-food restaurant for nearly a decade, believing the quiet hours were safe. That changed eighteen months ago when a customer began lingering near the drive-through window after closing, his face pressed too close to the glass, his eyes tracking her every move. Over three weeks, he appeared nightly, leaving notes tucked under windshield wipers, once a torn photograph of her walking to her car. The police were called; a restraining order was issued. But by then, the damage had taken root.

The memory of those nights had become a strange, fractured thing. Sometimes, when Layla was standing at the stove at home, she would catch a whiff of stale coffee and industrial cleaner—the exact smell of the restaurant lobby during those final shifts—and her stomach would drop before her mind had even caught up. At other times, she could replay the entire sequence of events in her head—the face at the window, the note fluttering onto her dashboard—and feel nothing at all, as though she were watching a stranger in a movie. The story itself felt unreal, too extreme to have actually happened to her, and this unreality only deepened her confusion about who she had become.

What frightened Layla most was the belief that if she allowed herself to think about the stalking in any sustained way, she would unravel completely. She had come to feel that she no longer knew herself; the woman who had once joked with coworkers and walked to her car without a backward glance was gone, replaced by someone brittle and watchful. This sense of lost identity fed directly into her vigilance. Because she could not trust her own mind to handle the memory, she began scanning the world for danger, and the more she scanned, the more dangerous the world appeared. She studied every face that came through the restaurant’s doors, reading body language for signs of fixation, certain that anyone could be the next person to follow her home.

The checking rituals started gradually. At first, Layla simply made sure her apartment door was locked before bed. Within weeks, she was checking it three or four times, then returning to the living room to confirm the windows were bolted. She began waking during the night, heart pounding, to listen for footsteps in the hallway. Each time she found nothing amiss, the relief was short-lived, because the very act of checking reinforced her belief that she was unsafe. And that belief, in turn, made the memories more vivid and more intrusive: she would be lying in the dark and suddenly smell the coffee and cleaner again, or see the photograph in her mind’s eye, and the cycle would tighten.

Her husband, a retired mechanic, grew frustrated. He would lock the door himself and tell her it was done, but Layla could not stop. She had come to believe that people could not be trusted—not strangers, not coworkers, not even the neighbors who waved hello. This mistrust bled into her work life. She requested only day shifts, which meant fewer tips and more conflict with the schedule manager. Her earnings dropped. When the manager asked why, she could not explain that she was terrified of the dark now, that the late shift had become a landscape of potential threat.

What finally brought Layla to seek help was a morning in late October when she found herself standing in her own kitchen, refusing to open the refrigerator door because she thought she heard breathing on the other side. She stood there for ten minutes, paralyzed, before realizing that the sound was only the old compressor. It was in that moment, with her hands shaking and her husband calling her name from the next room, that she understood she could not keep living this way. She was afraid of what she might become if she did not find a way out—more than that, she was afraid that the woman she used to be was already gone for good.
